name: WorkOS
summary: APIs that make a SaaS app “enterprise-ready”: SSO over SAML and OIDC, SCIM directory sync, a hosted login (AuthKit), audit logs and authorization.
intro: When a startup’s app starts selling to large companies, their IT teams ask for the same list: staff must sign in through the company’s identity provider (single sign-on), accounts must be created and removed from the company directory (SCIM provisioning), and security teams want audit logs. WorkOS sells each of these as an API. Its SSO service speaks SAML and OIDC to any identity provider but presents your app with one OAuth-style flow: redirect the user to WorkOS, get back a code, swap it for a normalised user profile. Directory Sync turns SCIM and HR-system feeds into users, groups and webhook events, and the Admin Portal is a hosted setup page where the customer’s IT admin configures their own connection, so your engineers don’t have to on a call.

On top of that sits User Management with AuthKit, a hosted, customisable login page with passwords, social logins, magic links and MFA, plus organisations, roles, fine-grained authorization and audit logs. The pricing splits the same way: User Management is free up to 1 million monthly active users, then $2,500 a month per extra million, while SSO and Directory Sync are charged per customer connection, $125 a month each for the first 15 with volume discounts after that.
strengths: Built around B2B needs: SAML and OIDC SSO, SCIM provisioning and audit logs behind one API
The Admin Portal lets each customer’s IT admin set up their own SSO and directory connection
Free hosted login up to 1 million monthly active users
Per-connection pricing maps to revenue: you pay for SSO when an enterprise customer needs it, regardless of how many of their users sign in
limits: Connection fees add up for many mid-sized customers: 15 SSO connections cost $1,875 a month at list price, and Directory Sync is billed separately
A hosted, closed-source service; your login depends on WorkOS being up, and leaving means migrating users and connections
Custom domains for AuthKit and the Admin Portal are an extra $99 a month

source: // 1. Send the user to their company's identity provider (SAML or OIDC)
// 2. In the callback: swap the one-time code (valid 10 minutes) for the user's profile
const { profile } = await workos.sso.getProfileAndToken({ code, clientId });

story: Michael Grinich co-founded Nylas, whose email app, Nylas Mail, users loved but large companies wouldn’t adopt: it had never been built for the enterprise IT admins who actually buy software, with their requirements for single sign-on, provisioning and audit logs. Nylas shut the app down and pivoted to infrastructure for sales tools. Grinich later gave a talk called “Crossing the Enterprise Chasm” to warn other startups, and in 2019 started WorkOS to sell those enterprise features as an API, which he described as “Stripe for enterprise-ready features”.

WorkOS launched in 2020 and quietly raised a $15 million Series A that year, led by Lachy Groom, an early Stripe employee; it announced the round in March 2021, by which time more than 100 apps, including Webflow and Hopin, were built on it. In November 2023 it moved into general authentication with AuthKit, an open-source login UI built on Radix with a hosted version free up to one million users, a market where it already pitched itself as an alternative to Auth0.

choices.choice: One API in front of every identity provider
choices.why: Each enterprise customer brings a different IdP, often over SAML. Normalising them behind one OAuth-style flow and one profile shape means an app integrates once instead of once per customer.

choices.choice: Let the customer’s IT admin configure the connection
choices.why: Setting up SAML or SCIM usually means certificates and URLs exchanged over email or calls. The hosted Admin Portal gives IT admins step-by-step guides for their own provider, taking the app’s engineers out of the loop.

choices.choice: Charge per connection, give login away
choices.why: Enterprise features are worth most when an enterprise deal closes. Pricing SSO per connection ties the cost to that revenue, while free AuthKit up to a million users draws in apps before they need it.
